title: India's US Envoy Kwatra Accuses Pakistan of Dismantling Indus Waters Treaty Over Five Decades
excerpt: In a Newsweek article, Ambassador Vinay Mohan Kwatra defended India's decision to hold the 1960 water-sharing agreement in abeyance, saying Pakistan's state-sponsored terrorism eroded the treaty's foundation of goodwill.
body:
• India's Ambassador to the US Vinay Mohan Kwatra published a Newsweek article arguing Pakistan spent five decades dismantling the goodwill underlying the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty.
  • Kwatra said India's decision to hold the treaty in abeyance merely acknowledged what Pakistan's conduct — including state-sponsored terrorism — had already destroyed.
  • He accused Islamabad of using the Indus dispute as a "distraction policy" to deflect from its terror infrastructure, and demanded its dismantlement as a precondition for any treaty restoration.
  • The statement is the strongest public articulation by a senior Indian diplomat on US soil of New Delhi's position linking water cooperation to counter-terrorism.

India's Ambassador to the United States, Vinay Mohan Kwatra, has launched a pointed public defense of New Delhi's decision to keep the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, accusing Pakistan of systematically eroding the 66-year-old water-sharing agreement through decades of hostility and state-sponsored terrorism.

In an article published in Newsweek magazine, Kwatra wrote that the Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960 "in the spirit of goodwill and friendship" — and that Pakistan had spent the subsequent five decades dismantling that very foundation. India's decision to suspend its obligations under the treaty, he argued, "merely acknowledged what Pakistan's conduct had already destroyed."

A Diplomatic Offensive on American Soil

The Newsweek article marks a notable escalation in India's public diplomacy around the Indus dispute. By publishing in a major American magazine, Kwatra is making India's case directly to Western policymakers and opinion-shapers — an audience Pakistan has also been courting with its own narrative of "water weaponisation."

Kwatra accused Islamabad of pursuing a "distraction policy," using the treaty dispute to divert international attention from Pakistan's continued harboring of terrorist groups and infrastructure on its soil. He demanded that Pakistan dismantle its terror infrastructure as a precondition before any discussion of restoring the treaty could begin.

"The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in the spirit of goodwill and friendship. Pakistan spent half a century dismantling it."

— Vinay Mohan Kwatra, India's Ambassador to the US, in Newsweek

Background: From Pahalgam to Abeyance

India placed the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance in April 2025, shortly after the Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 26 tourists. The decision, endorsed by the Cabinet Committee on Security, was the first time New Delhi had suspended its obligations under the World Bank-brokered agreement, which had survived three wars and decades of hostility between the nuclear-armed neighbors.

The treaty, signed under World Bank mediation, allocated the eastern rivers — the Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej — to India, while the western rivers — the Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab — went to Pakistan, with India permitted limited use for hydropower, domestic, and agricultural purposes. India surrendered roughly 80 percent of the Indus system's waters under the arrangement.

Since the suspension, India has also launched Operation Sindoor targeting terror hideouts, rejected what it called an "illegal" arbitration ruling on the Kishenganga and Ratle hydroelectric plants, and maintained that all measures will remain in place until Pakistan takes "credible and irreversible" steps to end cross-border terrorism.

Pakistan's Response and the International Dimension

Islamabad has rejected India's position, with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif accusing India of "weaponizing water" and putting millions of Pakistani lives at risk. Pakistan has sent multiple letters urging treaty restoration, taken the matter to the UN Security Council, and warned that any disruption to its water share would constitute a red line.

Pakistan's agriculture sector, which contributes 24 percent of its GDP and employs nearly 37 percent of its workforce, is heavily dependent on the western rivers allocated under the treaty. Analysts warn that a prolonged suspension could deepen Pakistan's existing water stress and food security vulnerabilities.

India, however, has shown no signs of relenting. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reiterated in July 2026 that the treaty "stands in abeyance" and that Pakistan must "credibly and irrevocably abjure" support for cross-border terrorism before any change in India's position.

Diaspora and Strategic Messaging

Kwatra's decision to publish in Newsweek rather than an Indian outlet underscores New Delhi's effort to shape the narrative among Western audiences, including the influential Indian-American community. The article frames India not as an aggressor withholding water, but as a nation that honored a lopsided agreement for six decades until the other party's conduct made it untenable.

"Blood and water cannot flow together."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on the link between terrorism and the Indus Waters Treaty

What's Next

With India accelerating hydroelectric projects in Jammu and Kashmir — including the Sawalkote, Ratle, and Pakal Dul dams — and exploring water diversion proposals, the treaty's future remains deeply uncertain. Pakistan's attempts to internationalize the dispute through the UN Security Council have so far gained little traction, with India arguing the council lacks jurisdiction over a bilateral treaty with its own dispute mechanisms.

The diplomatic standoff appears locked in place: India insisting on an end to terrorism as a precondition, Pakistan demanding the separation of water rights from security disputes. In that deadlock, Kwatra's Newsweek salvo is less an opening for negotiation than a statement of position — aimed squarely at an audience beyond South Asia.
nri_angle: Kwatra's Newsweek article represents India's diplomatic messaging to Western audiences, including the influential Indian-American diaspora, framing the treaty dispute as a security issue rather than a water rights question.
